speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Finance a question which I directed to the Prime Minister last week and which he promised to look into. In view of the statement by the Minister of Industry in a speech in Montreal to the effect that the Canadian economy is not growing fast enough to provide sufficient employment opportunities for

the growing labour force, and in view of the fact that the figures just published show that the gross national product for the last quarter did not increase substantially and that the non-farm sector declined slightly, does the minister plan to introduce any emergency measures to stimulate the growth of the economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY INDUSTRY MINISTER RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, dealing with the middle part of my hon. friend's statement about the growth of the gross national product, I would point out that in reply to a question from the Leader of the Opposition last week or the week before, I explained that the gross national product for the second quarter of this year was some 8.2 per cent higher than for the corresponding quarter a year ago, so that any suggestion that there has not been growth needs a little explanation.
In the way the statistics came out there was a statement to the effect that there had been no increase in the second quarter over the levels of the first quarter. This was because of the various policies designed to push some of the activities that normally occur in summer back into the winter months, to relieve unemployment during the winter. But I can assure my hon. friend that the economy would seem to be going along at a very satisfactory clip. I have said on other occasions that we do not expect the figures will show an upward surge in the quarter that ended in September, but we do expect a further upsurge in the last quarter, the current one, and it seems probable that the total increase for this year over last year will be of the order of 8 per cent.
In these circumstances I do not think any crash emergency programs are called for, although I can assure my hon. friend that the officials of my department and I are working on various measures that might be needed if the economy should turn up too far or if it should turn down, but at the moment there is no sign of that.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: WORLD FAIR
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXPRESSING CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY COMMISSIONER GENERAL
speechtext:
On September 17, Mr. Speaker, I gave a preliminary answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere regarding the government's intention in relation to Mr. Robert Shaw, deputy commissioner general of the Canadian corporation for the 1967 world exhibition. On that occasion I said I had asked the board of directors of the corporation for their views. On September 29 I received from the commissioner general the text of a resolution approved unanimously by the board the previous day. This resolution reads as follows:
In reply to the Minister of Trade and Commerce's invitation the board of directors wants to express its full confidence in Mr. R. F. Shaw, deputy commissioner general of the 1967 world exhibition.
Immediately on receipt of this resolution I conveyed it to my cabinet colleagues and to the Quebec government. With the concurrence of the Quebec government, the Canadian government has decided it is in the

Inquiries of the Ministry interests of Expo '67 that Mr. Shaw should remain as deputy commissioner general. This decision was made after a careful examination of the judgment and evidence in a recent case involving the Foundation Company of Canada.
As I have already said, Mr. Shaw has done an outstanding job as deputy commissioner general, and it is the government's view that his continuation at his post is very much in the interests of the success of the exhibition.

maintopic: WORLD FAIR
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXPRESSING CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY COMMISSIONER GENERAL
speechtext:
Can
the minister advise the house if this resolution by the board of directors of Expo '67 was obtained under a threat of resignation by the commissioner general, Mr. Dupuy, as is reported apparently authoritatively in Le Devoir?

maintopic: WORLD FAIR
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXPRESSING CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY COMMISSIONER GENERAL
speechtext: I cannot say anything about the accuracy of the report which appeared in Le Devoir and which I have seen. I was not present at the meeting. I simply asked the commissioner general to ask the board of directors their views. He reported to me in terms as I have reported to the house, and he informed me that this resolution was approved unanimously.

maintopic: WORLD FAIR
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXPRESSING CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY COMMISSIONER GENERAL
speechtext: I have a further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In anticipation of the minister's estimates, will he kindly inform himself on the question I have raised so we may not get the same kind of general answer on that occasion?

maintopic: WORLD FAIR
subtopic: RESOLUTION EXPRESSING CONFIDENCE IN DEPUTY COMMISSIONER GENERAL
speechtext: I would welcome any discussion of this matter during my estimates. I think it is most important to the success of the exhibition that not only the government but everyone concerned should have full confidence in Mr. Shaw.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subtopic: HAL BANKS-CONSIDERATION OF FURTHER CRIMINAL CHARGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all I can say on this point is that all the facts have been considered by two very eminent counsel, Mr. Robinette and Mr. Maxtineau. speechtext: On a point of order, I think I ought to correct the impression left that in the commission report of Justice Norris there was evidence upon which charges were to be laid. speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, October 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-121, to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates-Mr. Hays- Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
When the committee rose last evening clause 3 of the bill, with an amendment thereto by the hon. member for Acadia, was under consideration. Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment?

On clause 3-Loans to farm machinery syndicates.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
I will not delay the desired vote on this amendment for more than a few minutes. The whole of clause 3 and the amendment thereto deals with the question of the security to be set against the amount of the loan offered. The Minister of Agriculture has clouded the issue by repeated references to the fact that a person signing a promissory note for the total amount would not necessarily need to have sufficient security to cover the total amount for which he signed. But before I moved my amendment last evening I asked the minister whether a person whose total net worth was $5,000 would be able to sign a promissory note for the total amount borrowed by a syndicate of which he was a member, an amount of perhaps $45,000. I asked the minister whether the corporation would take a promissory note in those circumstances and place a value on it.
As reported on page 8757 of Hansard the minister replied "I do not suppose we would lend money to an individual in that position". I then asked what would happen in a case of a person who had total assets for security purposes of $15,000 and who wished to join a syndicate with three other members. Would his promissory note for $45,000, the total amount the syndicate wished to borrow, be accepted? To this question the minister replied "I think I must reply in the same fashion". In other words he did not think the corporation would lend money to an individual with a net worth of $15,000 who wished to join a syndicate borrowing $45,000.
It is a well known fact that the Farm Credit Corporation considers the question of security against loans to be of the utmost importance. Yesterday it was stated that a farmer could borrow $55,000 from the Farm Credit Corporation and another $15,000 from the banks under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I hesitated to make any suggestion that this might not be the case; I wanted it to come from the minister or his officials. But under part III of the legislation governing the Farm Credit Corporation the corporation can only lend a farmer $55,000 provided he meets all the requirements. One of the conditions is that the farmer must clean up his notes at the bank; he must have no other outside debts. In other words if a farmer who has borrowed $10,000 from the bank under the terms of the Farm Improve-
Farm Machinery
ment Loans Act applies for a loan under part III of the farm credit legislation, whether for the full amount or for less, he must immediately set aside sufficient money to meet his obligation at the bank.
I am pointing this out in order to convince the committee that no one is being fooled on this question of security. Despite all that has been said, we are all aware that when money is lent, even if the Minister of Agriculture is acting as the banker, as he has suggested, through the Farm Credit Corporation, adequate security will be insisted on, security which has not been pledged to cover another debt. I say once again that under the clause we now have before us, in the provision stating that a farmer must sign a promissory note for the total amount borrowed by a syndicate, such a promissory note must have the full amount of security backing.
I have put forward an amendment which may cause some difficulty, but it would have the effect of making the promissory note apply only to the amount of the loan applicable to each member of the syndicate, which seems to me much more sensible. A person with assets of $15,000 could then join a syndicate which wished to borrow $45,000; his share would be $15,000, and thus he could join in borrowing the total amount. As it is now, whether a syndicate is formed of three, six or seven members, each member has to sign for the total amount borrowed. This amendment if accepted would give the clause a much wider application and make it possible to cover many more small farmers who are perhaps in need of greater borrowing power.
I have nothing more to say, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Agriculture has considered this amendment; his officials looked at it all last evening. I have made my plea for a wider application of this bill so it will be applicable to the small farmers who have not the capital assets that the minister stated many farmers have. In his remarks last evening the minister said that in his part of the country they use $50,000, $60,000, $75,000 or $100,000 worth of credit at the banks. I hope we are not passing legislation to aid farmers who can already borrow $100,000 at the bank. I hope we are trying to pass legislation that will help farmers who can perhaps borrow $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 at the bank, and who need a little more credit to assist them in their operations.
If the Liberal party and the minister cannot visualize now how clause 3 will be dis-

Farm Machinery
criminatory against the small farmers, I have very little hope for them in the future, or for the small farmer as long as the minister stays in power. Yesterday the minister said he had 12 lawyers working for him. He could not help throwing in the odd little boast as to what a great man he was. He said, of course, that none of them were any good. When one considers this bill it looks as though the minister knew more than all the drafters, because it is certainly a hodgepodge.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to just register my strong objection to one feature of clause 5. This is the clause which says that the interest rate will be prescribed by the corporation. I think this is most unsatisfactory. I believe the minister indicated the other day that the interest rate would probably not be more than 6 per cent; I think that was the figure he gave. However, there is no guarantee in passing this legislation as to what the interest rate will actually be, not only at the moment but what it will be over the years, if it is left to the corporation. The minister keeps saying that this legislation is primarily to help small farmers. Certainly if it is to help small farmers I am enthusiastically in favour of such a measure. But if it is to help small farmers, surely we ought to be keeping the cost to the barest minimum, because it is the small farmers who need help.
A survey which has just been completed by the Ontario federation of labour produced some interesting statistics. They pointed out that 71 per cent of all the farmers produced and sold farm products with a gross value of less than $5,000, and that 46 per cent produced and sold less than $2,500 worth of farm produce in 1961, the last year for which complete figures are available. This means that in 1961 more than two fifths of the farmers of Canada had a gross income of less than $2,500. I leave it to anyone to figure out what their net income was; I suspect it was something less than $1,500.

It is these small farmers who need help. It is these small farmers who cannot buy the expensive machinery which would enable them to farm economically. It is these small farmers whom I hope the minister is going to encourage and assist in the forming of syndicates so they can buy machinery which will provide a lower per unit cost of operation.
It is perfectly apparent that farmers whose gross income is less than $2,500 a year and whose net income is probably less than $1,500 a year are going to need all the help they can get. When a farmer comes under the Farm Credit Corporation legislation the interest rate is stated in the act, as I remember, at 5 per cent. When the farmer borrows money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act the interest rate is stated in the act; again, as I recollect it, at 5 per cent. But here is legislation which the minister claims is directed primarily at assisting the small farmer. How is it going to assist the small farmer? He is going to pay interest, the minister says, of not less than 6 per cent.
Just look at the financial burden which will be placed on a farmer who goes into one of these syndicates. I am thinking of a small farmer. First of all he has to find his share of 20 per cent of the cost of the machinery. He must also sign a note, not only for his share but for the entire amount of money that is borrowed. He must also, at the time the loan is made, pay a 1 per cent service charge. In addition to this, the minister indicated yesterday that he will probably be expected to have fire insurance, liability insurance and life insurance to protect the syndicate in the event that any one of its members dies.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext: And a service charge of 1 per cent.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
I mentioned the service charge of 1 per cent at the time the machinery is purchased. If anyone wishes to add this up, I suggest this is not legislation designed to help small farmers. These farmers will be carrying a very heavy burden. The minister spoke yesterday about farmers buying machinery and paying 10 per cent and 12 per cent interest in this connection. I would think the government ought to have taken action long ago on that type of exploitation. The farmer here is going to pay very heavy costs, and I think the least the government can do is to give the farmer who is borrowing money from the Farm Credit Corporation under this bill terms at least as generous as those accorded to the farmer who borrows money

under the Farm Credit Act or under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
If the minister is desirous of helping small farmers it certainly is not apparent in this bill, particularly having regard to the wording of clause 5. I think by comparison to the minister Scrooge looks like a generous person. I say that because the burden which will be saddled on the small farmer who goes into one of these syndicates is going to be extremely heavy.
I would urge the minister to introduce an amendment to clause 5, as was done by the previous government in other farm lending legislation, to fix the interest rate in this clause, and that it will be 5 per cent. I think the government can borrow money at less than that rate, and if they cannot and this requires a subsidy, then the government is even more justified in subsidizing small farmers than it is in subsidizing farmers who borrow money under the Farm Credit Act or under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I hope the minister will see fit to either prescribe in the bill that the interest rate will not be more than 5 per cent or that he will give us some better explanation for leaving this item wide open than anything he has given us so far.

I do not think they would tend to fool me. There is another figure which the federation of agriculture came up with, I believe, a figure of something like $400 million, but I used the conservative figure of $240 million.
I am sure there is not a farmer in the country who would object to paying 6 per cent if he could purchase the machinery he needs, particularly when it is realized that over the period of the contract he is only paying one third of this 6 per cent, as he now has an opportunity to share this machine with three people or more. If he had to buy his own piece of equipment to do the work he would bear the full amount, but he will now have an opportunity of using a large machine on which he will actually be paying only 2 per cent, or one third of 6 per cent, if the capital cost of the contract works out as we anticipate it will.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a strange kind of arithmetic on the minister's part. The minister says a farmer will pay only one third of the 6 per cent interest; but he would only have a one third ownership in the machine, so he will pay the full 6 per cent on the part of the debt for which he is liable.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member was listening to me. What I said was this. Supposing the farmer had to buy the whole machine and pay, say, $10,000. He would pay 6 per cent interest on that machine. He now has an opportunity, if he need only use the machine for a small part of the time, to get exactly the same amount of work out of the machine by paying possibly one third of the capital cost. He would also only pay his share of the interest rate, which I know would be 6 per cent on his particular share; but his operating cost would be decreased by two thirds.

Farm Machinery

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
Well, we would all agree that the operating cost is less because the farmer is going into joint ownership of the machine. But he would only have the right to a one third ownership of the machine and to a one third use of the machine. Consequently he would not pay the same amount he would pay if he owned the machine completely and had the use of it all the time. That is the purpose of this legislation.
Surely the minister can give us a better reply than saying that the provinces could subsidize this interest rate. We are passing federal legislation. We have been repeatedly told by the provinces, and with a good deal of justification, that they have been called upon over the years to assume more responsibility than their financial revenues will permit, and all the tax rental arrangements have been designed to siphon off more revenue to the provinces and more taxes to the provinces in order that they may discharge their responsibilities. It is the federal government which has the money, and I do not think they should say that if the interest rate is too high the provinces can put up the money. The provinces in which this legislation will be most needed-I think particularly of the Atlantic provinces-are the provinces which can least afford to subsidize the minister's program. The minister wants to be Santa Claus and hand out presents providing somebody else pays part of the cost. Anyone can be Santa Claus on that basis, but this will not fool anyone. The farmers are holding the minister responsible, and the minister will be held responsible if the farmers have to pay 6 per cent when they borrow money to purchase machinery for these syndicates.
What the minister has not explained is why in this legislation the rate is 6 per cent and in other legislation it is 5 per cent. The farm improvement loans money is also short term; why is the interest 5 per cent in that case? If that money can be borrowed at 5 per cent there is no reason why this money cannot be borrowed at 5 per cent. And usually the amount borrowed will be a larger amount. If the minister is going to make the rate 6 per cent, then let him at least put it in the bill at "not more than 6 per cent", although I think it should be not more than 5 per cent, the same as in the other lending legislation. If the minister thinks that is too low let him put in the words "not more than 6 per cent"; then it would at least be stipulated in the bill. The farmers as well as the members of this house have no way of

knowing now whether this rate will creep up to 7 per cent or 8 per cent. There would be some protection for the farmers if the maximum rate of interest to be charged were stipulated in the statute. I know the minister keeps saying: Let us put the legislation into effect and try it out for a while, and then I will refer the legislation to the agriculture committee next year and it can be overhauled then. That does not solve the problem for the farmers who come under this legislation in the course of the next 12 months. If during the next 12 months farmers come under the legislation, enter into agreements with an interest rate of 6 per cent plus a 1 per cent service charge, make themselves jointly and severally responsible for the entire amount of the loan and as a result find themselves in a financial hotbox, amending of the legislation at the next session will not benefit them. It will benefit farmers who come under the legislation subsequently but it will not benefit farmers who come under the legislation between the time it is passed now and the time it is amended at the next session of parliament.
I predict that unless the minister re-examines some of the things he has put in the legislation there will be a great many farmers who in desperation will come under the legislation in order to get machinery, and will find subsequently that they have assumed a heavier burden of financial responsibility than they are able to discharge. I just do not see how a farmer with a gross income of less than $2,500 a year-the survey by the Ontario federation of labour shows that 46 per cent of the farmers of Canada are in that category-can afford to pay 6 per cent interest, a 1 per cent service charge, sign a promissory note to cover the entire borrowing of the syndicate and in addition carry fire insurance, public liability insurance and life insurance as a member of the syndicate. It seems to me this is a financial burden that small farmers will not be able to carry and some of them will find themselves in financial difficulties. I urge the minister to reconsider his decision and to put the maximum interest rate in the legislation, 5 per cent if possible or 6 per cent if he feels he cannot accept the 5 per cent figure.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, taking up the train of thought advanced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam I would say that the provision contained in subclause 2 of clause 5 is quite a reversal of the philosophy of farm credit legislation now on the statute books. This is going back to the rough, tough

days of the farm loan board. We all know why a new act was introduced and the Farm Credit Corporation was established. The purpose was to infuse into the whole farm credit field an entirely new philosophy, and I think it has been quite successful because the officials of the corporation are interpreting the act that way.
I would prefer to see this legislation simply say 5 per cent because it is quite as easy for the government to finance the operations of the Farm Credit Corporation with respect to this legislation as it is with respect to its general credit operations. I do not see why it should be more expensive to borrow under this legislation than under the Farm Credit Act.
Second, under the wording of subclause 2 the rate of interest is not fixed at all from year to year. The subclause reads in part as follows:
-at such rate prescribed by the corporation as in its opinion is sufficient to return to it an amount equal to the cost to the corporation of any money advanced to it for the purpose of making that loan-
That is a flexible amount.
-and the expenses of the corporation in administering that loan-
That is also a flexible amount.
-including a reasonable reserve against losses.
That is the third barrier. Therefore the corporation in its wisdom may start out with an interest rate of 5J or 6 per cent but two years later they may say they have to have an additional 1 per cent, so two years from now the rate will have gone up.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext: Or down.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
Or down. That is conceivable, but the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd) will readily understand that these rates do not usually go down. They usually go up because costs and reserves for losses are involved. But there is a third objection. The changing of the rate is not subject to restriction by regulation. The words used are "at such rate prescribed by the corporation". Clause 9 deals with regulations and provides that the corporation may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations prescribing the terms and conditions that a syndicate agreement must contain and defining the expressions "farm machinery" and "co-operative farm association". I would say that under a reasonable interpretation of clause 5, subclause 2, as it now stands the approval of the governor in council would not be required for a
Farm Machinery
change in the interest rate. By that I do not intend to impute improper motives to the corporation, but unless the minister can prove me wrong I want to point out that a reading of clause 5 and clause 9 together leads me to say that while all other regulations made initially under the act or later amendments are subject to the approval of the governor in council, it is not indicated that the interest rate is included.
I offer these alternatives to the minister. First of all, I should like to see a specific rate of interest prescribed in the bill. If it is found later that with the rate so fixed the Farm Credit Corporation cannot conduct operations successfully, then the corporation will have to come back to parliament for approval of any change. I think that is what should be done here if this legislation is going to be good legislation. It should be on a par with the Farm Credit Act. Therefore I should like to see the rate prescribed so that it will be clear.
Second, if that is not acceptable I should like to see it clearly stated that the rate prescribed by the corporation is subject to the approval of the governor in council. That should be stated clearly in clause 5. There is what I consider to be a latent ambiguity in the language and I think my doubt is sufficiently well founded in the imprecise language in clause 5. If what I have suggested were done there would be a further check.
My first recommendation to the minister, in line with what the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam has said, is that the interest rate should be spelled out right here in the clause. If you are going to make it 5 per cent, say so. If it is going to be 6 per cent, say so. Second, let us have it clearly set out that any change in the rate of interest shall be subject to the approval of the governor in council. In that way there would be a much closer retention of supervision by parliament over the operations under this legislation.
In saying this I am not imputing improper motives or actions to the Farm Credit Corporation. As a matter of fact, I think we would remove from their backs the burden of approving an interest rate, a burden which I think should rest here in this house.

speechtext:
I hesitate to enter this debate because I come from a clan of logsplitters and not hairsplitters. After listening to this debate, I just wonder what the farmers of this nation are thinking. I am a farmer, and I know that over 50 per cent of the money that is borrowed in this nation is borrowed at high interest rates, much higher than we will be setting under this bill, from modern day Shylocks and from bonus merchants. This bill will overcome these practices to a great extent. When my own family started farming, and we were a large family, we had nothing like this bill on which to rely. We had to borrow money from whoever would lend it. We did pool our assets to buy our equipment for farming.
As I said earlier, this measure is of tremendous advantage to the average young farmer in this nation. So far as I am concerned, this interest rate is all right. I, as a farmer, approve of it. I do not believe we should go around this nation yelling for lower interest rates just because we are farmers. The farmers of this nation, as I

have said before and I will say again, are the most efficient producers in the world. The people of this nation are enjoying the cheapest food, when food prices are related to their earning power, of any nation in the world. I feel we should be able, as the minister has said to make these crops return sufficient to the farmer so that he does not have to go around like a second class citizen asking for special privileges in the way of interest rates. I feel we are actually professional people, industrialists or whatever you want to call us.
Yesterday I heard the hon. member for Acadia pleading the case of the small farmer. In the area from which I come we are small farmers and we do not farm several thousand acres. I know what the small farmers want. I know how important this legislation can be to them. In our area there are many small farmers such as onion producers and vegetable producers, who are being put out of business because they cannot compete with the money people who are taking over this part of the business. The small farmer is being eliminated, and this is an important way of life to many of these people. I visited the countries of Europe last year and I saw that the incentive was taken away from people when these farms were incorporated. The individual farmer's incentive to produce no longer existed. We must preserve the right of the individual farmer to be an independent farmer.
We know that farmers can work together through their co-operatives. We know they can work together to purchase machinery and equipment or whatever is necessary in their everyday life. As a result of the buoyant economy in my area during the last two years, a lot of young men are leaving the farms. This is one of the most productive areas in Canada or in North America. These young people are leaving the farms because they cannot compete with the money people in obtaining credit. As I said earlier, if we had had a bill such as this available to us when we were trying to start a farm we would have been able to enjoy a better way of life. We would have been able to compete with farmers who had unlimited capital to play around with. While we were sharecropping and doing everything possible to make ends meet, others had credit facilities available to them. I say that we in agriculture today, no matter where we may be in Canada, should be able to pay the going rate of interest and should be able to accept our place in society as first rate citizens.

So far as I am concerned, there has been too much talk in connection with this bill, too much delay. It annoys me, as a farmer, and as a farmer who had to help himself. Last year I introduced a bill to protect farmers against bankruptcy. The same people who say they are worried about what is going to happen to the farmer under this particular bill are the ones who held up my bill. They did not want to protect the farmers.

In most cases the farmers go broke too, because they have overcapitalized in this machinery by trying to buy it themselves. There is no bill like this right now to protect the farmers.

speechtext: Why didn't the government bring it in, then?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER

speechtext: This bill, so far as I am concerned, bars a close relationship to what I was trying to do last year. Many of our farmers are operating on returns that do not give them a fair way of life. The bill I was introducing last year attempted to give them protection under the old system of borrowing money from Shylocks to buy equipment. If they lost their crops, they were not able to pay anything. The same people who are complaining about the bill before us today are the ones who talked against my bill and did not want to give the farmers protection. So far as I am concerned this measure is long overdue.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
I do not want to hold up clause 5, but I do subcribe to some of the arguments made by the hon. member for Essex South as well as to some other things the Minister of Agriculture had to say with regard to farmers wanting to stand on their own feet. I wonder if the minister would consider with me the arguments respecting this matter of interest rate from a slightly different angle? Clause 5 refers to the corporation setting the appropriate rate that will take into consideraion the expenses involved in the corporation administering the loan, including reasonable reserves against losses. In addition to that, another clause we are about to consider refers to an additional service charge of 1 per cent per annum on the loan. Now, we have not any indication as to how high this is all going to add up, or what the final figure will be. We
Farm Machinery
feel it is going to be somewhere around 7 per cent. Perhaps this is substantially lower than some of the interest rates now being charged by lending institutions for loans on farm machinery; but under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which has been operating since 1945, and under which hundreds of millions of dollars have been lent to farmers, the losses to date have been approximately only one tenth of 1 per cent.
Under the provisions of this bill, where security is guaranteed jointly and severally by all members of a syndicate, there is a higher interest rate to be charged. This greater security must lower the risk factor, but on the other hand the interest rate will be substantially higher than the 5 per cent charged under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. For that reason it does not seem reasonable that there should be a higher rate of interest.
Another point is that we have staff within the Farm Credit Corporation to administer this bill, and it seems unreasonable that another charge should be made on the proposed loans for administration. It may be that the corporation will need staff-I do not deny that-but the same principle applies to all government operations whether in farm legislation, in unemployment insurance or in transport. Staff is already being paid by the public treasury and no charge is made for the administration.
As I have said on a number of occasions, though I am concerned with some of the bill's provisions I am prepared to let it pass on a trial basis, and a year from now we can refer it to a committee, find out what weaknesses it has and try to deal with them. Time and again the minister has said the major purpose of this bill is to assist small farmers to buy large, expensive pieces of machinery that they require, under terms by which they would own it and use it cooperatively, thus reducing the cost of the machinery.
I believe a simple amendment to the Farm Improvement Loans Act would allow farmers to borrow up to $15,000, both independently and jointly, for the purpose of buying farm machinery. The limit of loans under that act was raised to $15,000 a month ago, so that any farmer who had used up to his previous maximum of $7,500 now has another $7,500 available to him if he qualifies under the provisions of the act. Amending that act would have been a simpler and more effective way of meeting the needs of small farmers, because $15,000 is a substantial amount,

Farm Machinery
particularly when one is speaking in terms of a very small farm.
To some extent I support the argument advanced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Edmonton West that a specific rate of interest should be prescribed by this bill. An interest rate of 5 per cent has been set for loans under other farm legislation, and since the loans to be made under this bill will be better secured than individual loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, I see no justification for a service charge of 1 per cent over and above the cost of money to the Farm Credit Corporation. Nevertheless, I do not take any hard objection to this because I think the increased maximums provided under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which were passed by parliament last month, will meet farmers' needs for the next few months. I think these maximum amounts will be used, because loans under that act will be approximately 2 per cent cheaper than credit provided by this bill.

Certainly clause 5 makes it quite clear that the interest rate must take into account such things as an amount equal to the cost to the corporation of any money advanced to it, also the expenses of the corporation in administering loans, and a reasonable reserve against losses.

speechtext:
May I say briefly that I support this legislation in principle. It has proven successful in Great Britain and Scotland, operated by hard headed farmers in the United Kingdom, supported by the national farm union and the co-operative societies which are related to the agriculture industry there.
This is an experiment. We are applying to Canadian conditions provisions which have been successful in England and Scotland. I fully appreciate the criticisms which have been advanced from the benches to my right and I support some of them. I refer to the fact that co-operative organizations are not allowed to borrow; that some of the regulatory features have not been included in the bill, and that there should be a fixed interest rate. As I say, I appreciate these criticisms. But I wish to read two or three paragraphs to indicate what has been done in this field in the United Kingdom. I am all in favour of giving this scheme a trial for a year and finding out where the kinks are, and straightening them out as a result of experience.
I intend to read from an article entitled "Farm Machinery Syndicates" written by Mr. N. L. Goodland. This is what it has to say:
A machinery-buying syndicate, having been accepted as 'creditworthy', may consist of two farmers or more. On approach to Syndicate Credits Ltd.-
That is the organization which supplies the capital.
Farm Machinery
-80 per cent of the cost of the article may be loaned, the remaining 20 per cent to be paid by the syndicate on delivery. The loan so made is paid off in half yearly instalments, with interest payable only on what is outstanding. Loans for movable equipment may be paid off over four years and this may be extended to five years in the case of grain-drying, storage and cleaning plants.
Further costs are made up as follows: Syndicates Credits Ltd. are charged 1 per cent on money borrowed and also an initial levy of two pounds sterling per syndicate member, which goes back to the agricultural central co-operative association to cover the cost of administration.
Syndicates Credits Ltd. are also charged for loans one half per cent above bank rate. The syndicates themselves are charged a further 1 per cent to cover the country's administrative costs.
This is similar to the provision included in the bill before us.
Thus the rate of interest charged to each syndicate is L per cent above bank rate, between the limits of 5 per cent and 7 per cent, calculated on outstanding balances only.
I do not intend to read any more from this article, now. The adjustment comes in the profit to the members of the syndicate at the end of the year-the savings. I suggest it would be ideal to have a fixed rate of interest, but I presume that if as the result of one year's operation of the act it was found unnecessary to charge the interest rate which had been fixed-if a reserve was developing-the rate could be lowered. I simply say therefore that I do not think we should continue a lengthy debate on this bill. We support it in principle though we criticize some of the details. We look upon it as an experiment in Canada based on successful experience in other countries. Let us pass this measure, give it a trial, and find out what happens at the end of the year.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief. I have already made plain during the one or two interventions I have made in this debate that I was greatly concerned at the fact that in clause 9 this parliament is being asked to delegate to government the exclusive right to settle the main characteristics and essentials of this legislation, and not only to settle them initially but to alter them from time to time as the case may be. I am not going to repeat the arguments I made in this regard; I would simply say that as this debate has progressed it has become quite apparent that we who take this view are correct.
During the course of the resolution stage questions were asked of the minister and he said that when we had the bill before us we would have the answers. This was quite proper, because the bill at that time had not been exposed to view. Then on second reading stage of the bill he said that when we got into committee we would have the specific answers. But when we got into committee we found that although some of the answers were given, the main features of the bill which are of most consequence and importance were buried in the right of the governor in council to approve the regulations of the corporation.
I think this principle is undesirable. It is not a new principle. The minister and his officials are probably proceeding in the light of the experience of governments over a great many years. Step by step, stage by stage and act by act parliament is being asked to give to government the right to exercise the functions which parliament should exercise, and that is a practice to which I for one would take exception. I think it is quite wrong. It would have been easy for the minister and his officials to define what is meant by farm machinery. I think that if it stood by itself I for one would not ask for a specific definition of that phrase; I think there is an accepted understanding of what is meant by farm machinery. Even if "co-operative farm association" were left I think wa could probably accept it. But when there is added to those two features of the bill the right of the corporation to prescribe the terms and 
conditions which a syndicate agreement must contain before it is approved by the corporation, I must draw the line.
In order to test the feeling of the committee concerning the extent to which we are being asked in almost indecent haste to give these powers to the government, I should like to move the following amendment to this clause:
That clause 9 be amended by adding after (c) the following:
"provided however that any regulation made under this section shall cease to have any force or effect unless approved and ratified by parliament within six months from the date such regulation comes into effect".
Before I sit down let me say I put the term "six months" in the amendment because the minister indicated that he hoped to bring the legislation back to this house. He admits that it is new and experimental and he suggests that he might bring it back in a year. I would be prepared, if the minister accepts the amendment, which would mean that any regulation which he makes must be brought back to this house for approval, to change "six months" to "one year", which would then meet the condition he has laid down.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 9(a) says the corporation may make regulations prescribing the terms and conditions that a syndicate agreement must contain before it is approved by the corporation. This is the only difference so far as the Farm Credit Act is concerned. That clause was put in the bill so that there would be flexibility to enable the syndicates to fix their own agreements. These agreements may be different one from another. Their application may be different. F'or instance, farmers in Prince Edward Island would probably invest in a mixing machine and would be entirely different from the farmers who would invest in summer fallowing equipment which is used in western Canada, where one outfit would summer fallow 2,000 acres at the rate of 150 acres a day. This wording would allow the corporation to examine the agreements.
I did cover this matter the other day but I will go over it again. I think it would be better if I read the explanation because the other day I was hurrying along and probably some hon. members did not have the opportunity to examine the explanation in Hansard. We believe there are excellent reasons and excellent precedents for this approach. The most obvious reason is that this provides greater flexibility in dealing with

farmers' applications for loans under this bill. But a precedent can also be found in the Farm Credit Act, again a precedent approved by parliament and well proven in actual operation. We believe this is the only sound approach we can take to ensure that the program, a new and experimental one, can be revised and improved as experience dictates. Besides leaving the definition of "farm machinery" to the regulations, the Farm Credit Act in section 11 confers other rather extensive discretion on the Farm Credit Corporation. This discretion, which is not subject to approval by governor in council, includes the authority to prescribe the forms of mortgages and agreements which farmers make with the corporation. I believe this was one occasion when the previous government showed a lot of common sense.
I am convinced, and I am sure everyone familiar with the great variety of the farmers' credit needs would agree, that this kind of flexible approach is essential for success in any farm credit program. This is why we have proposed that the items to be covered in agreements under the farm machinery syndicates bill should also be left to the administrators, to the people dealing directly with the farmers.
Naturally we have given very careful consideration to the general terms which the regulations will require in the agreements. Farmers forming a syndicate will have to make provision for such items as the rights and liabilities of syndicate members, including the interest in it of each member; insurance of the property against fire, and of the syndicate against public liability; the addition of new members; the withdrawal, death, insolvency, retirement or incapacity of a member for any cause; the dissolution of a syndicate; the holding of syndicate business meetings; the election of syndicate officers; the procedures in the event of default by an individual syndicate member; maintenance and sale of machinery; keeping proper records and accounts.
These are some of the general terms. But I am sure hon. members would not want to dictate to farmers in advance every detail as to how each syndicate must organize to meet these general terms. In administering the program, of course, the Farm Credit Corporation will suggest various ways in which these general terms can be met. For example, suppose a member wants to withdraw from a syndicate because he has sold his farm, or does not need the machinery any longer for some other reason. A syndicate agreement
Farm Machinery
could include a provision for any member to withdraw as long as he could make a mutually satisfactory arrangement with other members to take over his share of both the assets and the liabilities, or for another farmer acceptable to the other members to take his place. In other words, since he would have an equity in the net worth of the syndicate he would be able to dispose of it to the remaining members or probably to another farmer. The farmers themselves might like to make other arrangements.
By leaving the terms and conditions of agreements under this bill to be set by regulation by the administrators, we provide the farmers with the freedom to make any reasonable arrangements they and the corporation see fit to make.

Mr. Chairman, clause 9 purports to give authority to the Farm Credit Corporation to make regulations defining the expression "farm machinery". In my opinion it is pretty difficult to define farm machinery and I think that the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River is very worth while indeed. The minister has repeatedly told us that the legislation is experimental and that he wants to put it on trial for a year. In his amendment the hon. member for Peace River has suggested six months, but if it is agreeable to the government he is willing to change it to 12 months.
Before the vote is taken may I say I am somewhat disappointed that the minister has not given us a wider view with regard to this point. He has had the officials before him and he says they have studied the bill for nine months. I am surprised he is not able to give us a wider view as to what the bill will cover so far as farm machinery is concerned. At various times I have listed what I thought was farm machinery and what I thought the bill might include, but the minister has failed to comment on most of my suggestions.
We have accepted the principle of the bill, which is that farmers can join together in syndicates and by so doing economize in carrying on their farming operations. First of all you have farmers joining together to form a syndicate so that they can economize in carrying on their farming operations. This should be the main theme when considering what is or is not farm machinery. No attention whatsoever should be paid to the definition laid down by the Department of National Revenue that machinery must have moving parts. This should not enter into the thinking 
of the officials at all because any machine should be permissible as long as the farmers are carrying on farming operations and can economize and cut down their costs by forming a syndicate.
I have suggested silos or buildings but the minister has not commented on that suggestion. According to the dictionary a machine is a contrivance put together to do a piece of work. This is roughly what the dictionary says about the definition of a machine. I can see many possibilities for farmers to form marketing syndicates. In Prince Edward Island today there are literally hundreds of marketing syndicates or farmers' co-operatives through which the farmers market their produce. I see no real reason why farmers should not form such syndicates if they want to advance their produce one step farther toward the marketplace. It has often been said that farmers need more power in the marketplace. This legislation could be of tremendous help to groups of farmers who wanted to establish their own marketing set-up.
The agriculture committee is studying the feed grain problem. I suggested in the committee that many farmers could build elevators in their own localities and instead of moving their grain to the lakehead and down through the waterway when it is cheap and plentiful, they could store it in their elevators and distribute it among themselves during the winter months when they most need it. Would a huge farm storage bin purchased by a syndicate qualify as farm machinery?
We have never had an answer to this question of whether or not buildings qualify as farm machinery. I believe this bill could be of great benefit in many localities in eastern Canada in which farmers are feeding livestock. I know that in my own area many livestock are fed on grass. I can think of a number of instances in which much of the land is held under a grazing lease. A lease is a machine, a contrivance put together by human beings. I believe that that is a logical explanation of the definition of machinery. Certainly a group of farmers could form a syndicate and purchase a lease. They will be economizing tremendously in this way.
I recall that a lease was sold near my place not long ago to the Calgary stampede. I know the minister is aware of this particular transaction. They paid $84,000 for this grazing lease. If the ranchers in that area had been able to form a syndicate and each borrow $15,000, they would have readily purchased that grazing lease. It would have been of tremendous help to these small farmers. I see

some possibility for this legislation if the definition of farm machinery is broadened. It is for this reason I heartily concur in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River. Let us have a look at the definition of "farm machinery". I have suggested it should include silos, grain elevators, feed mills, grazing leases, and so on.
Why should the potato farmers of Prince Edward Island or any other part of Canada not be able to form a marketing syndicate for marketing their farm product? Why should they not have the benefits of this legislation? Why could they not erect a warehouse or a system for washing, cleaning and chipping their potatoes? Why should farmers not be able to do these things? Is this not the direction in which farming is moving today? Farming is becoming more mechanized and farmers are moving their produce closer to the markets. The fact is that the minister has failed to give the committee any broad statement concerning the regulations and the definition of farm machinery. The best he could do was to read a prepared statement that he made yesterday, and that is hardly good enough.
I know the minister is aware of this purchase by the Calgary stampede board to which I referred. I know this particular bill could be of direct benefit to many farmers in that area if they were able to borrow money and purchase a grazing lease. What is the difference between feeding cattle on grass or feeding cattle in a feed lot? In both cases we hope the cattle are getting fat and we hope there will be a market for them once they are ready for sale. The minister has said that a portable feed mill would come within the regulations. I asked him about a stationary feed mill for which one would pour a concrete floor. He could not comment on that because no one gave him a prepared statement. I ask him now about the feed grain situation in eastern Canada. Can farmers form a grain storage syndicate to store enough grain for their winter use in close proximity to their farms or feed lots? Can they build a grain storage elevator under this syndicate bill? Can they build stationary silos or set up a feed plant under this bill? Will the minister make an effort to see that a broad definition of farm machinery is established so that this bill could truly be, in the minister's words, as flexible as possible?

I think the government has been making a serious, determined effort to try and meet the needs of the farmers. Their needs are essentially for financial assistance to enable them to bring their farm operations up to a state of efficiency which will allow them to reduce costs and remain competitive. This is not a problem unique to farmers; it extends to other areas of the economy.
However, one must bear in mind, in providing assistance, what the law is; and about this I know something. There are two kinds of security, either under the civil law or the common law. One is security related to real or immovable property, and the other is related to movable property, or chattels. Something that is a structure and is attached to the soil is an immovable or real property and is not, and cannot be, the object of a chattel mortgage. This whole bill is designed to make available credit to farmers, or syndicates of farmers, on the sole strength of the security of the chattel itself, the movable piece of equipment, the farm machinery. The house resumed from Wednesday, September 16, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Hays-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Crop Insurance Act to authorize the governor in council to enter into agreements for the purpose of establishing a crop reinsurance program to supplement provincial crop insurance plans: to provide for the establishment in the consolidated revenue fund of a special account, to be known as the crop reinsurance fund, to which shall be credited amounts paid by a province under a crop reinsurance agreement and out of which shall be paid amounts required for the payment of reinsurance claims; to authorize advances from time to time from the consolidated revenue fund by way of non-interest bearing loans to the crop reinsurance fund; and to authorize the rebate, to grain growers whose grain is grown on insured lands, of sums paid by way of levy under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Crop Insurance Act AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose on the evening of September 16 I had only had about three or four minutes to express some views respecting the resolution before us. I do not want to take a great deal of time this evening in attempting to examine the whole field of crop insurance for Canadian farmers in all the various areas and for all the different types of operations throughout Canada. I do, however, think it is worth repeating, as has been said before in the house a number of times, that the crop insurance schemes set up by three of the provincial governments on a pilot project basis have been something less than successful. In other words, if these pilot projects were to provide the experience and direction necessary to institute a complete and comprehensive crop insurance scheme they have not succeeded in doing so at least up to this time. So I think we will have to be patient while these crop insurance schemes evolve and until either the provincial governments or the federal government are prepared to embark upon a complete and comprehensive insurance scheme that will provide insurance and income to farmers all over Canada in case of crop failure.
The resolution before us represents a forward step. I think one of the reasons why the provincial governments have been a little timid in expanding their crop insurance schemes is that there was the overhanging possibility of being faced with a crop disaster year when a great deal of crop was under the insurance scheme, with the result that their resources would be taxed beyond their capacity to meet the payments if such an occurrence took place. It may be that new information will come to the attention of provincial governments over the years on the basis of the experience they gain respecting these matters. We know that up to the present time the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba have tried crop insurance on a very limited scale. We know that Prince Edward Island has also proceeded to take what has been referred to as a very timid step. At the last session of the Alberta legislature enabling legislation was passed so that that province too can establish a pilot project.
As I said, I think the action of the government to provide for reinsurance is a good move from the point of view of assisting the provincial governments if they should en-

counter what might be termed a tragedy year. But what I am even more concerned about while we are gaining experience is the suspension of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in those areas where crop insurance schemes are established. We have had 25 years of experience in evolving a plan not necessarily of crop insurance but at least of a type of payment to farmers in the three prairie provinces today you will find that failure. Certainly this experience has caused the federal government to recognize the weaknesses and to introduce amendments to the act from time to time to take care of those weaknesses. If you go to many parts of the prairie provinces today you will find that the farmers are reasonably well satisfied with the operations of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. In saying that, Mr. Chairman, I am not suggesting it is perfect. I think it could be still further amended so that it would in fact be a form of insurance rather than simply a payment when disaster strikes.
We in this party believe that we could perhaps use the administration developed under P.F.A.A. to good purpose in embarking upon the much wider field of crop insurance. So far as the resolution before us is concerned, it requires complementary operative legislation passed by the provinces before it will have any effect at all. I am not entirely sure in my own mind whether this is the responsibility of the provinces. I know that a fairly good argument can be made on the basis of the varying types of conditions in the different provinces or regions of Canada, and perhaps it would be better if programs were developed in such a way as to take into consideration the specific conditions existing in a region. Perhaps that argument has some validity. On the other hand, under P.F.A.A. we already have a rather large organization with offices established and experienced personnel in several of the provinces and certainly we should not disregard their experience. Before I would be prepared to suggest that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is completely successful I would say we have to recognize there are some improvements required in the administration of that act as well. I had intended to go into considerable detail about this because the resolution calls for the suspension of the P.F.A.A. wherever crop insurance schemes are set up.
During the last few days I have noticed another resolution on the order paper, No. 78, which in fact calls for referring the royal commission of inquiry into the P.F.A.A. to the committee on agriculture. I believe that

would be a more appropriate time to deal in detail with some of the changes that ought to be made in the administration of the P,F.A.A. Tonight, Hr. Chairman, I do want to say this: during the past few months we have had a very serious cloud cast over the administration of the P.F.A.A. across Canada because of certain actions that took place in this house and a committee of this house. I believe that there ought to be an opportunity to present the other side of the coin to the Canadian people so they will not believe this Prairie Farm Assistance Act is some kind of political pork barrel, and a few other things, as it was called in Time magazine of August 7. There are weaknesses, and serious weaknesses, but one of the most serious weaknesses recently in the administration of the P.F.A.A. has been the fact that persons in responsible positions have stood in the way of punishing those who chose to abuse the regulations of the P.F.A.A. This, Mr. Chairman, is something that needs to be corrected.
There is an editorial in the Western Producer of August 27, 1964, which reads in part as follows:
The P.F.A. Act is a sound piece of legislation, of immense help to farmers in dry years. We cannot see it being supplanted in this area by more comprehensive crop insurance for a long time to come. It is therefore of supreme importance that it be administered and used fairly and honestly by all concerned. And let those who are not concerned, meaning all but the farmers and the properly constituted administration and the minister in charge, keep out of it altogether.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is a rather profound statement coming from a paper that has its circulation primarily within the area in which P.F.A.A. is operative. I should like to quote one paragraph from Time magazine for August 7:
The Pope report found that there were indeed "irregularities in the Swift Current situation which reverberated all the way to Tory agriculture Minister Hamilton's office. According to the judge's version of the story, McIntosh "had a very profound influence" over P.F.A.A. Swift Current supervisor George Walker, and he put pressure on Hamilton and his executive assistant, Roy Faibish, to get the election-time cheques out quickly. Left in charge of the matter, Faibish prevailed on the P.F.A.A.'s board of review to clear the cheques although the P.F.A.A. directors had argued that they should be held up while the doubtful claims were investigated.
There are more and more of these. I have an editorial from the Edmonton Journal dated August 14 which supports my contention that the recommendations of this Pope royal commission ought to be referred to either the committee on privileges and elections or the committee on agriculture.

I do not believe I have been out of order in anything I have said up until this time, because if you read the resolution carefully

you will see it is a substitute for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and I am trying to point out that that act has been successful except in those areas where it has been abused. Further, how I can develop that argument, without referring to some of the quotations that were widely used across the country during the last six or seven weeks, is beyond my comprehension. I realize there will be an opportunity to discuss this matter later in the session whenever item No. 78 on the order paper comes up for debate, and at that time we will be able to discuss the Pope report and all matters respecting the abuses of the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. For that reason I will not pursue the matter further tonight.
In closing I suggest that if it is the intention of the government to reinsure provincial crop insurance schemes from time to time, with a view to the eventual suspension of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, it is a mistake. This act has 25 years of experience behind it. Over the years numerous amendments have been made to it, changes have been made in the regulations and in the amount of the levy farmers pay, and all these were undertaken to ensure it continued to do the job it was designed to do. I shall express myself in much more detail on this when item 78 comes before the house.
Over the last 25 years the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has cost the treasury an average of less than $10 million a year to guarantee some return to all the farmers in the three prairie provinces. It has taken the tragedy out of complete loss from failure of crops, and has been one of the cheapest and best federal programs fox protecting a large group of Canadian citizens from tragedy.
When there is a good crop year, such as there was in 1963, the farmers pay a large amount of money back into the fund through their 1 per cent levy. I do not say they completely restore the fund, or that the fund has been actuarially sound for the past 25 years, but no other federal assistance program, in agriculture, unemployment insurance, freight rate subsidies, or whatever you care to name, such as subventions for coal, has given the same security to as large a group of people as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and at such a low price.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on resolution No. 49 now under study. This resolution is of interest not to us, but to the western provinces. We are pleased that it has been introduced.
It is noteworthy that not very long ago we were promised a crop insurance scheme for eastern Canada, as we were also promised a department of agriculture for eastern Canada; but a perusal of this resolution shows that the crop insurance scheme for the east will suffer the same fate as the department of agriculture for eastern Canada.
As can be seen, this resolution deals with the signing of agreements for the establishment of a crop reinsurance program to supplement provincial crop insurance plans.
As far as Quebec is concerned, it will not be difficult to supplement the provincial plan, because we have no such plan at present.
Our province has absolutely no crop insurance program even though people have been talking about it for years. Eastern farmers, especially those from Quebec, are still expecting the federal parliament or the provincial legislature to set up a crop insurance scheme adapted to the needs of the province.
A little further, toward the end, the resolution reads as follows:
-to authorize advances from time to time from the consolidated revenue fund by way of noninterest bearing loans to the crop reinsurance fund: and to authorize the rebate, to grain growers whose
20220-558i
Crop Insurance Act
grain is grown on insured lands, of sums paid by way of levy under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Now in the text of this resolution the province of Quebec has been entirely forgotten, and I think the minister is doing the same thing himself.
It seems to me that it is contrary to normal procedure to levy taxes indirectly in order to come to the assistance of the western provinces. We are delighted to see that they have finally got a crop insurance scheme in the west which, although it may not be 100 per cent satisfactory to them, is improving little by little. But in the province of Quebec we are still awaiting the day when this act will be passed.
Various areas of the province have suffered losses this year; in my area apple orchards have suffered; elsewhere other sectors of agriculture have sustained losses. I know some farmers who at the present time are completing provincial government claim forms, who completed such forms a year ago, two years ago, and who have not received a red cent.
Not later than yesterday morning a farmer came to see me. All his apples were destroyed by frost this fall, and the federal government's resolution contains absolutely no provision for assisting this apple grower or, in the Beauce area, the maple syrup producers, the raspberry, strawberry or various garden crop growers.
When this resolution is considered by the committee on agriculture, I should like the minister to add to it a few paragraphs having in mind the province of Quebec and eastern Canada, and to take into consideration other products than grain. Grain is an important asset in our country but farming in Canada is not exclusively concerned with grain; farmers in eastern Canada are engaged in mixed farming.
In the last few years I know that some farmers have spent large amounts for seeding their land and who lost their crops for various reasons. The federal government could easily reimburse expenditures of that kind in the province of Quebec or in other provinces.
A farmer or an apple grower must spend two Or three months to maintain his orchard, his raspberry, and his strawberry patches; he may spend from $2,000 to $3,000 hoping that he will have a crop in the fall. But when he loses everything, it seems that the federal government could create out of this crop reinsurance fund, a fund to compensate

Crop Insurance Act
the farmer for expenditures incurred in seeding or cultivating his orchard.
Mr. Chairman, it seems very difficult for the present Minister of Agriculture, as it was for his predecessors, to set up a crop insurance scheme which would be in the interests of the province of Quebec or of eastern Canada.
Our crops are diversified, and we are proud that the farmer belongs to our national heritage and can grow such fine products. However, at present no provision in our laws will assist the province of Quebec and take into consideration the conditions of its agriculture. Such legislation does not exist.
Since this is a resolution it is impossible to further discuss the program of crop reinsurance, but I wish that the minister would consider reimbursing essential expenditures to farmers who lose their crops. It costs $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 yearly to maintain an orchard; seeding costs some of our farmers $2,000 or $3,000. It would be easy to provide for the reimbursement of the essential outlays, when they have put in the crop.
Mr. Chairman, it might seem complicated but it is not. Until now we have never given thought to crop losses in eastern Canada and I see, on the government benches, good Liberal members who during the last electoral campaign promised a crop insurance. I do not know whether they intended it then for western Canada only, but from their speeches it seemed to me that they meant agriculture in eastern Canada.
It is time to add a few paragraphs to this resolution to ensure that the Quebec farmers are not completely forgotten.

Mr. Chairman, before the resolution carries I have one or two things I should like to say, although I might be a little sidetracked in view of the previous remarks. I should like to draw to the attention of the committee some matters which

concern my particular area of Canada as well as Canada as a whole. As I understand it, crop insurance and crop reinsurance applies to Canada as a whole. Provinces almost from coast to coast are considering taking advantage of this legislation. However, there is some doubt in my mind about this word "reinsurance". For example Alberta has no insurance agreement at the moment. I am very much in favour of crop insurance and reinsurance, but in view of the position in Alberta I should like the minister to explain how there can be "reinsurance" in a province which has no insurance to begin with.
Another point which comes to mind is a little more basic. This is a program for general crop insurance which, as I have just said, I am very much in favour of. I am particularly in favour of this bill because its provisions would apply from coast to coast as agreements are reached between the provincial governments and the federal government. I am disappointed that Alberta is apparently dragging its feet in reaching some agreement with the federal government; perhaps Alberta is one of the provinces which is asking for reinsurance before there is even any insurance agreement.
Some of these matters have been touched on in connection with a previous bill, but I find it rather hard to amend legislation before it is even put into effect and tried. In my particular area of Alberta as well as in other areas across the country it would be easy to institute a crop insurance program. I am not too sure why certain provinces are dragging their feet but as far as Alberta is concerned one reason must be that there is no crop insurance in force in the province at the moment. All too often Canadians have to have things all wrapped up with a blue ribbon before they will even look at them. I think Alberta should have taken part in this scheme earlier, and I hope the minister will even go so far as to put on record why we have to make provision for reinsurance before some provinces even have insurance.
Much has been said about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and I should like to say something in defence of P.F.A.A. Although I have had many complaints about P.F.A.A. in my area I do not think this is due to any faults in the legislation itself. Something which we in this committee should guard against at all times, and be jealous of, is the fact that after passing legislation we often find some difficulty in giving it recognition, purely because between the time it becomes law and its application in the field many
Crop Insurance Act
rules and regulations are appended thereto. We try to anticipate these rules and regulations in this house, regulations which in many cases are much needed; but the fact remains that the addition of rules and regulations makes it hard actually to recognize the original legislation. Sometimes these rules and regulations change the whole meaning of the act. Perhaps it is time that the rules and regulations in connection with P.F.A.A. and the legislation itself were amended, much in the same way as other legislation throughout the years comes up for revision in order to simplify it, to clarify it and to bring it back to earth.
If I may return to the subject of crop insurance and reinsurance for a moment, I have heard it suggested here that we should consider raising the levy against grain growers for the purposes of P.F.A.A. I should like to say that I am definitely not in favour of that. I should like to point out why, and try to relate my reasons to the resolution before us providing for a crop reinsurance program. Some areas have long term averages of, say 20 bushels to the acre over a period of 30 to 40 years. Let us say that the gross price throughout those years has been $1.50 a bushel or $30 an acre. One per cent of that is 30 cents an acre. This is the gross, not the net figure, and if you take 30 cents an acre for a 20 or 30 year period you have $6 or $9 an acre. Actually no benefit whatever has been received and even at today's prices the amount of money paid represents the price of a good amount of crop insurance.
I have no real complaint on that score but I do have a complaint about raising the levy for any purpose unless it is for an improvement. I can recall several years when if I had realized 1 per cent of the gross- you can figure out what that is when you get down to the net-or 2 or 3 per cent of the net I would have thought I was doing very well on my investment. I want to say very definitely that I am not in favour of raising the P.F.A.A. levy as suggested by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether in fairness the hon. member would also say that I suggested the awards be raised correspondingly?
