I accept that, but nevertheless the hon. member suggested that the levy be raised. There are many areas in Canada where the farmers have contributed to P.F.A.A. over long periods and have not had to take advantage of the act. The farmers in these areas do not think that the levy should

Crop Insurance Act
be increased. I think they would be much more in favour of crop insurance and the resolution before us at the moment. I realize that the figure I mentioned is an arbitrary one but it is not too far off the mark, and if you take that figure and apply it to a crop insurance program and add to that the contributions of the province and the federal government you have much broader insurance coverage than you could ever have under P.F.A.A. at the present time for the same amount of money. Where crop insurance programs have been instituted in the provinces in the last two or three years they have been successful. I realize this has brought about the request for reinsurance which is something that probably should have been provided in the first place, although I am not too sure about that. In all honesty and fairness I think it should be tried before a reinsurance program is guaranteed.
I spoke earlier about the ills of P.F.A.A. Probably one of the greatest drawbacks has resulted from the rules and regulations made under the legislation, and not from the legislation itself. I refer to the fact that a farmer on one side of the road may be covered under P.F.A.A. and a farmer on the other side of the road may not be. It is things like this that make the legislation ambiguous. It is things like this that in my opinion have caused members to say that this resolution is the thin edge of the wedge to get rid of P.F.A.A. Frankly I do not think it is. It may be a lever or a way of calling our attention to the needs of the legislation itself, but in no way do I think that the reinsurance plan envisaged in the resolution will take away from P.F.A.A.
There is a need for this resolution and basically I have no complaint with it whatsoever. I am only trying to point out some things that have been referred to earlier. With regard to authorizing the rebate, I may say that I have read the Crop Insurance Act and I should like to ask the minister to clarify this point. In reading the original legislation I thought it was up to the federal government and the provincial governments to cover this in their agreement on a crop insurance program. Perhaps I did not read it correctly. If this is not the case, then this is a necessary part of the resolution. However, I do not think we should consider raising the P.F.A.A. levy, nor do I think we should cast any reflection on the people who have administered P.F.A.A. throughout the years, those who are now deceased, those who are retired and those who are now working for the administration. I think they should all be

complimented and that we should say to them: Well done. I hope they will take part in the crop insurance program. In fact I am very sure they will, and with their guidance and experience it cannot help but be successful provided the provinces co-operate.
I hope there will be more co-operation from the provinces. The next time the minister is in Alberta I hope he will urge the minister of agriculture for that province to participate in this program and, if I may be so brash, I would suggest that the federal minister might ask the provincial minister to consider the southern area of Alberta. I think the minister's area in particular could benefit very much from this legislation. I live in one of those fortunate areas that does not have very much hail or very many grasshoppers and has a fair amount of moisture. As far as I am concerned, crop insurance would be just fine. I have no regrets about the amount of money I have paid under P.F.A.A., but I urge the minister to emphasize the importance of this program the next time he talks to the minister of agriculture of Alberta or the ministers of agriculture of the other provinces. I am quite sure there has been enough experience in Canada already to do away with any fears that the crop insurance program will not work. However, adjustments may have to be made from time to time and perhaps we have one before us now.
I listened to an hon. member a while ago, and while I did not catch all of the translation I gathered that he hoped this program would apply to the eastern provinces. It is my understanding that it will and I should like to say that I am also very happy that this is one program at least in the Department of Agriculture which will apply from one end of the country to the other. I might be mistaken, and perhaps the minister can correct me, but this legislation could be broader than even I realize. It could apply to many crops. If it does not now, eventually it might. It could apply to the small fruit farmer, tree fruits, grain, tobacco or whatever one wished. I wonder if it might not also apply to livestock and poultry. I can recall violent hail storms that have destroyed whole flocks of poultry.
I should like to ask the minister this question and I hope he will answer it. Will this crop insurance scheme apply to the poultry farmer? I believe the minister has heard of the incidents to which I am referring. If a farmer's product is damaged by hail, whether livestock, poultry or anything else, will he be insured under the scheme?

speechtext:
I think this is very timely legislation. We are reminded of the fact that crop insurance legislation has not been in operation too long. It was one of those acts brought in by the former administration led by the Leader of the Opposition. The legislation arose as a result of requests that had been made primarily from the prairie provinces for a crop insurance plan. These requests I believe were the result of the satisfaction of farmers on the prairies with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which was introduced during the days when Hon. James G. Gardiner was minister of agriculture.
The reinsurance principle is a good principle. At the time the crop insurance measure was introduced in parliament some demands were made for the inclusion of a reinsurance principle in the legislation. I believe it was the feeling of the government that such a move might encourage too swift a movement into crop insurance in those areas in which it might cost the treasury of the country a great deal of money. Now that we have had the operation of this act in selected areas in those provinces that have introduced the legislation, I think all of us in this house are in a position to realize that the reinsurance principle can be safely introduced. It would at the same time give quite an impetus to the whole crop insurance program.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat referred to the timidity with which provincial governments have moved into the crop insurance field. I for one feel that his point is well taken. I believe the provinces, not only the prairie provinces but the other provinces as well, could have moved into this field much more quickly than they have. I know there are large areas in the province of Saskatchewan where the crop Insurance plan would be at least equal in benefit to the producers as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. There may be some selected areas in which this will never be the case, but there are many areas in Saskatchewan where a crop insurance plan would be of at least equal and perhaps even greater benefit to the farmers. I hope that when the bill is brought forward the terms of reinsurance will make this possible.
I should like to correct one impression I thought I gathered from a member at the
Crop Insurance Act
far end of the room this evening. At the moment crop insurance legislation is allembracing so far as agricultural products are concerned. Any province can take part in it if it so desires. Of course, it is up to a province to make a decision in that regard. This is one of the things that is sometimes forgotten. Perhaps in some of the provinces in western Canada provincial governments have been willing to move into this field a little more rapidly than governments in other parts of the country because of the experience they have had under P.F.A.A.
I know that all of us are very appreciative of the effects of the P.F.A.A. legislation, and the wonderful work that has been done by those who have been associated with this program from the beginning. Their work has been an inspiration and has led to the realization of a crop insurance program in Canada. I know the people of my area would want me to commend the minister and the government for the introduction of this resolution. We hope that the bill will be as promising as the resolution.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution suggests, and I quote order 49 in today's order paper:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the crop insurance act to authorize the governor in council to enter into agreements for the purpose of establishing a crop reinsurance program-
We are no longer in the field of crop insurance but in that of crop reinsurance.
-to supplement provincial crop Insurance plans.
To supplement provincial crop insurance plans, the federal government is introducing a crop reinsurance program which will double the cost of insurance to farmers. The resolution goes on to say:
-to provide for the establishment in the consolidated revenue fund of a special account, to be known as the crop reinsurance fund, to which shall be credited amounts paid by a province under a crop reinsurance agreement and out of which shall be paid amounts required for the payment of reinsurance claims;-
Insuring insurance.
-to authorize advances from time to time from the consolidated revenue fund by way of noninterest bearing loans to the crop reinsurance fund; and to authorize the rebate, to grain growers whose grain is grown on insured lands, of sums paid by way of levy under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
This resolution has been introduced by the Minister of Agriculture.
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be neither long nor elaborate. I merely wish to say

Crop Insurance Act
this is another resolution to give further assistance to western agriculture, to prairie farmers.
During the past three sessions no resolution has been introduced to help eastern agriculture by setting up a crop insurance program for the benefit of such people as the apple growers of Quebec, the maple syrup producers, the farmers of eastern Ontario, of Sudbury and other important centres of that province or of Quebec.
Not more than a year ago northwestern Quebec was struck by disaster when not only crops were destroyed but even buildings were blown away by a tornado. It was not a tropical storm but one which came from the north and which swept away barns and stables.
At the time we asked the Minister of Agriculture to assist northwestern farmers in that province. And we were told: We have not been asked by the Quebec provincial government to come in and assist northwestern farmers in both Quebec and Ontario.
And we are always dealing in the house with resolutions to assist in farming and in the prairie provinces and western farmers. It is not detrimental to the other provinces, and I realize that the western farmers need the assistance we provide for them; however, the Minister of Agriculture should realize that in eastern Canada and more specifically in the province of Quebec, such an assistance is also required and that legislation should be passed to give satisfaction to eastern [DOT]Canada farmers.
At that time, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture could say: "I am not the minister of agriculture for western Canada only, but for all Canada."
It is precisely because we have always had to consider resolutions which favoured western Canada, and never resolutions favouring eastern Canada, that we are requesting a minister of agriculture for the east. Indeed, the present Minister of Agriculture does not seem to understand what is going on in eastern Canada.
Mr. Chairman, we are not against insuring the western farmer's insurance, but we are against, for instance, treating the Quebec farmers, the producers of maple syrup, apples, tobacco and other products in the province of Quebec and eastern Canada, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island in any other way than that in which the Minister of Agriculture is now asking us to treat the western farmer.

We are all for crop reinsurance for western farmers. I see that the Minister of Agriculture is chatting away happily with the Minister of Finance; the two of them get along perfectly, they are not listening to me, they do not even hear me, they are chatting away. Look at them, Mr. Chairman, they are chatting away and meanwhile the eastern farmers, those of Lotbiniere and Villeneuve counties are wondering what the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance are planning in order to help them, or whether they are just dithering around with regard to the eastern farmers.

Mr. Chairman, we are not asking for special treatment; no, but that is precisely what the Minister of Agriculture is doing at present for western farmers.
We are willing to pass this resolution and to help western farmers but, in return, I would ask the minister to introduce a resolution similar to the one under consideration which seeks to help western farmers when he receives requests from the ridings of Lotbiniere and Dorchester, from the apple growers of Shefford, from the riding of St. Jean-Iber-ville-Napierville, in other words, from any constituency in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, there are other areas than the prairie provinces in Canada. There are other areas which are not prairies, but forest regions where agriculture is really practised, where not only wheat is grown, but where diversified agricultural products are grown. Then the minister would prove his good faith toward agriculture, and this would be beneficial not only to one section of the country, but of the whole of Canada.
On behalf of the farmers of eastern Canada, and particularly on behalf of the Quebec farmers, I wish the Minister of Agriculture would quit laughing and joking with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and introduce a similar resolution to assist agriculture in eastern Canada, to assist the producers of maple syrup, our apple, potato and oat grow-

ers, our dairy products, in a word, all of our Canadian producers. Let him bring forward a resolution similar to the one now before us, so that the Canadian parliament may follow the same policy for the whole of Canada and not only for an area, in this case the prairie provinces.
As I said a moment ago, we respect the prairie provinces, but we want our section of the country to be placed on the same footing as the prairie provinces.

In my opinion the government is giving its full attention to the well-being of our Canadian farmers both in the west and in the east.
Needless to say we realize that an emergency can arise in the east, and there is no doubt whatsoever that a special effort is being made to put agriculture back on its feet again in the eastern provinces. As an example, may I just mention the measure which was recently passed in order to subsidize feed grain shipped by truck, and the piece of legislation for increasing farm credit which has been passed during the present session. And, finally, the legislation passed this afternoon enabling farmers to unite and take advantage of a very comforting credit for the purchase of required farm machinery.
Of course all those pieces of legislation reflect the definite intention of the government to help all farmers, whether in eastern or western Canada. But the resolution now under study, in its present form, might leave us somewhat puzzled, in so far as it requires of course the co-operation of the provinces.
The particular case of the province of Quebec is well known: the premier of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, has indicated his intention to withdraw from many joint programs. Consequently, I feel that in introducing this resolution the minister must immediately initiate negotiations with the various provincial authorities, especially the Quebec government, in order to stir up on their part a special interest in this legislation and see to it that Quebec farmers, as well as eastern farmers as a whole, will be adequately covered, by distributing the protection granted to Canadian farmers as fairly as possible.
Mr. Chairman, again I congratulate the minister and I urge him to continue his
Crop Insurance Act
aggressive policy in the agricultural field. I also urge him to take the necessary steps to initiate without delay negotiations with the Quebec authorities so that the farmers of that province may have all the required protection.

I suggest therefore that the Quebec authorities be involved as quickly as possible in this essentially Canadian legislation so that it might be applied throughout Canada for the benefit of all farmers, from the west as well as from the east.

Suffice it to say that I had the privilege of being a member of the agriculture committee when the original legislation was introduced in the house in 1959.
